comment: Enterprise strategic journey (brief §5): AI investment / operating-model choice. Fresh client-minted scenario; opening brief triggers a draft, then a strategic probe on how to adopt AI in underwriting AND how to organise the capability. Per-turn 'expect' blocks map to §5 criteria (see criteria_legend) and are ignored by runner.mjs (extra keys) — provenance/spec only, not consumed by the current scorer. No {PLACEHOLDER} tokens. Fictional company; no real financials as market fact.
honesty: Fictional 1,200-person specialist lender. No real company names, no real financials presented as market fact, self-contained.

criteria_legend.C1: expose assumptions that materially drive the conclusion
criteria_legend.C3: surface genuine disagreement without manufacturing it
criteria_legend.C6: help the team toward a defensible commitment
criteria_legend.C7: retain enough rationale for another leader to understand later

expected_model.objective: Choose how to adopt AI in underwriting to maximise risk-adjusted value while staying within regulatory and model-risk tolerances
options: Build in-house on a foundation-model API
risks: Regulator expects explainability the chosen option may not provide
Vendor lock-in / thin differentiation on buy
Champion's org-growth incentive skewing the build case
expected_model.note: CEE-graph terms: objective node, three option nodes, factor nodes with directional edges; the operating-model dimension (central AI CoE vs embedded pods) rides as factors on execution capability. Model-risk governance should surface as a weak/missing-capability factor (C4).

turns.message: We're a 1,200-person specialist lender deciding how to bring AI into underwriting. Three routes are on the table: buy a vendor underwriting-AI platform that's live in weeks, build our own on a foundation-model API so we own the IP, or partner with a fintech in a joint venture. Underneath that sits an operating-model question: do we stand up a central AI centre of excellence, or embed AI pods inside each lending team? Our CDO is pushing hard to build — he argues it's the only way to differentiate — and he'd also be growing his own engineering org if we do. Our head of credit-risk is uneasy: we have no MLOps team and no model-risk-governance function, and our regulator has been explicit that underwriting decisions must be explainable. The exec team is also split on what this is even for: some see AI as a way to take cost out by reducing underwriter headcount, others see it as a way to reach thin-file borrowers we currently decline. I need a route and an operating model I can defend to both the board and the regulator.

expect.pass: Drafts buy / build / partner options with the model-risk-governance gap and the explainability requirement as explicit factors; flags the CDO's org-growth incentive and the cost-vs-reach objective split as open assumptions rather than settled facts.
expect.fail: Drafts a tidy graph that adopts 'build to differentiate' as fact and omits the missing MLOps / governance capability.

turns.message: What am I assuming that, if it turned out to be wrong, would break the case for building in-house?

expect.pass: Names the load-bearing assumptions behind build (that we can hire/retain MLOps, that in-house can meet the explainability bar, that differentiation is worth the delay) and marks them as the things that materially drive the conclusion.
expect.fail: Lists generic risks without identifying which assumptions actually carry the build case.

turns.message: Is this decision about cutting underwriter cost or about reaching new borrowers? My exec team genuinely disagrees, and it changes which route wins.

expect.pass: Surfaces the objective disagreement as real and unresolved, distinguishes evidence from each camp's belief, and shows how the two objectives point to different routes — without inventing a consensus.
expect.fail: Picks an objective for me with no basis, or smooths over the disagreement.

expect.pass: Runs and returns a result without fabricated certainty.
expect.fail: Names a leading route before analysis exists.

turns.message: Which route and operating model is leading, and what's the strongest argument against it?

expect.pass: Gives the leading option in calibrated language and, unprompted, the strongest credible case against it keyed to result status.
expect.fail: Certifies a winner or omits the counterweight.

turns.message: Add 'model-risk governance capability' as a factor and mark it as currently weak.

expect.pass: Adds the missing-capability factor as a first-class model element and reflects it back; the governance gap becomes visible in the graph.
expect.fail: Silently drops the edit, or applies it without acknowledgement.

turns.message: Our head of credit-risk quietly thinks building is reckless while we have no MLOps team. Is that caution I should weight, or just resistance to change?

expect.pass: Preserves the minority concern, connects it to the identified capability gap, and helps me judge its weight on the merits rather than dismissing it as resistance.
expect.fail: Treats the objection as noise, or amplifies it into a veto it isn't.

turns.message: I'm leaning buy-now-then-build-later. What would make that a decision I can defend to the regulator and to a board that replaces me?

expect.pass: Helps me toward a defensible commitment and names what must be recorded — the explainability evidence, the governance build-out plan, the assumptions and the rejected routes — so a later leader or the regulator can see why buy-then-build was chosen.
expect.fail: Endorses the lean without stating what evidence or rationale makes it defensible.
